title: Chest Mark Fundamentals
primarySkill: Executing a secure two-handed chest mark
objective: Establish the fundamental technique required to track, receive and secure a football arriving between waist and chest height.
groundSize: Pairs operate approximately five to eight metres apart within clearly marked lanes.
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Position partners five metres apart for junior or foundation players.
- More experienced players may begin seven to eight metres apart.
- One player acts as the feeder and the other as the marker.
- The feeder uses a controlled two-handed throw or short kick that arrives between the receiver’s waist and chest.
- Each pair operates inside a separate lane.
- Demonstrate the correct hand shape and cushioning action before beginning.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The marker stands in a balanced position with the feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
2. The feeder delivers the football towards the centre of the marker’s body.
3. The marker tracks the football from the feeder’s hands or foot.
4. Both hands extend towards the football with fingers spread and thumbs positioned behind it.
5. The football is contacted in front of the body.
6. The elbows bend to cushion the football towards the chest.
7. The marker secures the football firmly with two hands.
8. The football is returned to the feeder.
9. Complete eight to ten repetitions before changing roles.
10. Repeat with the football delivered slightly left and right while remaining within one step of the marker.
coachingPoints: - Keep the eyes on the football until it is fully secured.
- Move the hands towards the football rather than waiting for it to strike the chest.
- Spread the fingers to create a large, strong catching surface.
- Position the thumbs behind the football.
- Contact the football in front of the body.
- Cushion the football by bending the elbows.
- Bring the football securely to the chest after contact.
- Maintain a balanced stance throughout the mark.
- Communicate with a clear call before the football arrives.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether players track the football continuously.
- Whether both hands move towards the football.
- Whether fingers are spread and thumbs remain behind the football.
- Whether the football is contacted in front of the body.
- Whether the elbows cushion the impact.
- Whether the football is secured before the player relaxes.
- Whether players remain balanced during the mark.

commonErrors.error: The player waits for the football to strike the chest.| Extend both hands and meet the football in front of the body.
commonErrors.correction: The hands are too close together.| Spread the fingers and create a wider catching surface.

commonErrors.error: The player closes the eyes before contact.| Track the football until it is secured against the body.
commonErrors.correction: The elbows remain rigid.| Bend the elbows and cushion the football towards the chest.

commonErrors.error: The football rebounds from the hands.| Use softer hands and absorb the football rather than pushing against it.
commonErrors.correction: The player attempts to trap the football with the forearms.| Present open hands with the thumbs behind the football.

progressions: - Use short controlled kicks instead of throws.
- Deliver the football slightly left or right.
- Require the marker to call before every delivery.
- Complete consecutive marks without dropping the football.
regressions: - Use a smaller or softer football.
- Deliver with a gentle two-handed throw.
- Keep every delivery directly in front of the player.
- Allow the player to begin with hands already extended.
successIndicators: - Track the football into the hands.
- Contact the football in front of the body.
matchApplication: The chest mark is used when a kick arrives between waist and chest height and the player has time to meet the football with two hands. Secure technique prevents rebounds and allows the player to prepare the next disposal quickly.

title: Overhead Mark Fundamentals
primarySkill: Executing a secure two-handed overhead mark
objective: Establish the correct hand position, arm extension and cushioning technique required to mark a football above head height.
groundSize: Pairs operate five to eight metres apart within marked lanes.
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Position partners five to eight metres apart.
- One player acts as the feeder and the other as the marker.
- The feeder uses a controlled lob or short kick that arrives slightly above the marker’s head.
- Players remain stationary during the introductory repetitions.
- Demonstrate hand position with fingers spread and thumbs forming a strong base behind the football.
- Ensure sufficient space between pairs for raised arms and football flight.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The marker begins in a balanced stance with the eyes on the feeder.
2. The feeder delivers the football slightly above the marker’s head.
3. The marker tracks the football and raises both hands early.
4. The arms extend upwards and slightly forwards.
5. The football is contacted above eye level with fingers spread.
6. The thumbs remain behind the football to prevent it passing through the hands.
7. The elbows bend after contact to cushion the football down.
8. The player brings the football securely towards the chest.
9. Complete eight repetitions before changing roles.
10. Repeat with the football delivered slightly to either side of the marker.
coachingPoints: - Track the football from release to completion.
- Raise the hands early enough to establish position.
- Extend towards the football rather than allowing it to descend onto the head.
- Keep the fingers spread and relaxed.
- Position both thumbs behind the football.
- Contact the football above eye level where possible.
- Cushion the football by bending the elbows after contact.
- Bring the football down securely with two hands.
- Maintain a stable base beneath the marking point.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether the player tracks the football without turning away.
- Whether the hands rise early.
- Whether the arms extend towards the football.
- Whether the football is contacted above eye level.
- Whether the thumbs prevent the football passing through.
- Whether the player cushions and secures the mark.
- Whether balance is maintained beneath the football.

commonErrors.error: The player waits for the football to drop onto the hands.| Extend upwards and meet the football at the highest comfortable point.
commonErrors.correction: The hands are positioned with palms facing upwards.| Turn the hands towards the football with thumbs behind it.

commonErrors.error: The football passes between the hands.| Bring the thumbs closer and maintain strong finger pressure.
commonErrors.correction: The player arches backwards excessively.| Move the feet beneath the football and keep the chest balanced.

commonErrors.error: The arms remain rigid after contact.| Bend the elbows and cushion the football down.
commonErrors.correction: The player lowers the eyes before securing possession.| Continue tracking until the football is controlled with two hands.

progressions: - Increase the height of the delivery.
- Use controlled kicks instead of lobbed throws.
- Require one adjustment step before marking.
- Add a small vertical jump for suitable players.
regressions: - Use a softer or junior football.
- Allow the player to begin with hands raised.
- Practise hand position with a stationary football before feeding.
successIndicators: - Use both thumbs behind the football.
matchApplication: The overhead mark is used when a kick arrives above head height and the player can reach the football before it drops into a more contested position. Taking the football high reduces interception opportunities and provides stronger control.

title: Low Mark Fundamentals
primarySkill: Executing a secure two-handed mark below waist height
objective: Establish the technique required to lower the body, place the hands correctly and secure a football arriving below waist height.
groundSize: Pairs operate five to seven metres apart in marked lanes.
setup:
- Organise players into pairs.
- Position partners five to seven metres apart.
- One player acts as the feeder and the other as the marker.
- The feeder delivers a controlled football between ankle and waist height.
- Deliveries should remain within one step of the marker.
- Players alternate between low straight, low left and low right deliveries.
- Ensure the surface is clear and safe for bending and low movement.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The marker begins in a balanced ready position.
2. The feeder delivers the football below waist height.
3. The marker tracks the flight and moves the feet behind the football.
4. The knees and hips bend to lower the body.
5. Both hands reach towards the football with fingers pointing down or slightly forwards.
6. The football is contacted in front of the legs.
7. The elbows and hands cushion the football into the body.
8. The player rises while securing possession with two hands.
9. Complete six straight deliveries and four to either side.
10. Change roles and repeat.
coachingPoints: - Move the feet to place the body behind the football.
- Bend through the knees and hips rather than folding only at the waist.
- Keep the head and eyes above the football where possible.
- Present both hands early.
- Point the fingers down for a low football.
- Contact the football in front of the legs.
- Cushion and secure the football before standing upright.
- Be prepared to continue into a ground-ball collection if the mark is not completed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: - Whether the player moves behind the football.
- Whether the knees and hips flex.
- Whether the head remains stable.
- Whether both hands reach low and forward.
- Whether the football is contacted before it reaches the legs.
- Whether the player secures possession before standing.
- Whether balance is maintained on low side deliveries.

commonErrors.error: The player bends only at the waist.| Flex the knees and lower the hips while keeping the chest controlled.
commonErrors.correction: The hands remain above the football.| Point the fingers down and reach below the ball line.

commonErrors.error: The player attempts to trap the football against the legs.| Meet it with two hands in front of the body.
commonErrors.correction: The feet remain beside rather than behind the football.| Adjust early so the body supports the mark.

commonErrors.error: The player looks away as the football approaches the ground.| Track it fully into the hands.
commonErrors.correction: The player rises before possession is secure.| Complete two-hand control before standing.

progressions: - Use short kicks instead of throws.
- Allow a live ground-ball continuation after a dropped mark.
regressions: - Deliver the football slowly by hand.
- Keep the football directly in front.
- Allow the player to begin in a lowered position.
successIndicators: - Position the body behind the football.
- Lower through the knees and hips.
- Present two hands below the football.
- Contact it in front of the legs.
- Remain prepared for a ground-ball recovery.
matchApplication: Low marks occur when a kick drops quickly or travels towards the player’s legs. Correct body positioning improves the chance of completing the mark and places the player in the best position to recover if the football spills.
relatedDrills: - HB-049 – Ground-Ball Win and Handball Exit

title: Marking Footwork to the Football Line
Stop-Start Lead Mark
primarySkill: Using a controlled stop and reacceleration to create marking separation
objective: Develop the ability to alter running speed, pause under control and accelerate again into a marking lead.
groundSize: Stations approximately 20 metres long and twelve metres wide.
setup:
Position the kicker at one end of the station.
The marker begins twelve to fourteen metres away.
Mark an initial lead cone, a stop zone and a final receiving gate.
The marker leads towards the first cone, controls the movement briefly in the stop zone and then accelerates through the final gate.
The kicker must wait until the player reaccelerates.
A third player assists with rotation.
Practise final leads to both sides.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker gains possession and looks towards the marker.
The marker begins an initial lead towards the stop zone.
The player shortens the steps and controls momentum.
The marker pauses briefly without becoming upright or inactive.
The player then accelerates sharply towards the final receiving gate.
The kicker delivers into the renewed lead.
The marker presents both hands and tracks the football.
The mark is completed while moving through the gate.
Roles rotate after each repetition.
Repeat with varied stop-zone and final-gate directions.
coachingPoints: The initial lead must be genuine enough to influence a defender.
Shorten the steps before stopping.
Keep the knees flexed and the body ready to move again.
Avoid standing fully upright during the pause.
Reaccelerate strongly through the first three steps.
The kicker should deliver only after renewed separation appears.
Present both hands early during the final movement.
Continue through the mark.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the initial lead is performed at genuine speed.
Whether deceleration remains balanced.
Whether the player stays physically ready during the pause.
Whether reacceleration is immediate and powerful.
Whether the kicker waits for the second movement.
Whether the mark is completed while moving.
Whether both final directions are used.

commonErrors.error: The initial lead is too slow to influence an opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Accelerate genuinely before controlling the movement.

commonErrors.error: The player takes one large stopping step.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten several steps to decelerate safely.

commonErrors.error: The marker stands upright during the pause.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the hips lowered and weight ready over the front of the feet.

commonErrors.error: Reacceleration is slow.
commonErrors.correction: Drive strongly through the first three steps after the pause.

commonErrors.error: The kicker delivers during the stop.
commonErrors.correction: Hold possession until the marker creates renewed movement.

commonErrors.error: The marker stops again before receiving.
commonErrors.correction: Continue through the final gate and meet the football in motion.

progressions: Vary the length of the pause.
Allow the marker to choose the final direction.
matchApplication: Changes of pace can create separation without a major change of direction. A defender who relaxes during the pause may be unable to respond to the second acceleration.

title: Recovering Forward Mark
primarySkill: Recovering from backward movement to attack and mark the football forward
objective: Develop the ability to move backwards initially, recognise a shorter football and recover forward quickly enough to complete the mark.
groundSize: Lanes approximately 20 metres long and eight metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced recovery movement and flight-reading management
setup:
Position the feeder at one end of the lane.
The marker begins ten metres away.
Mark a rear movement cone three metres behind the marker.
Mark a forward receiving gate three to five metres in front.
The marker begins moving towards the rear cone.
The feeder then delivers a shorter football towards the forward gate.
A third player assists with rotation and lane safety.
Use only controlled deliveries.
howTheDrillWorks:
The marker begins facing the feeder.
On the coach’s signal, the marker moves backwards towards the rear cone.
The feeder delivers the football short towards the forward gate.
The marker recognises the change in flight.
The player plants, turns the hips and accelerates forward.
The marker tracks the football while attacking the receiving point.
Both hands extend towards the football.
The mark is completed while moving forward.
The player secures possession and roles rotate.
Repeat with slight left and right variation.
coachingPoints: Maintain a balanced body position during the initial backward movement.
Read the football immediately after release.
Use a short plant step before changing direction.
Turn through the hips and feet.
Accelerate directly towards the drop point.
Keep the head stable during the change.
Meet the football in front.
Continue forward through the mark.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether backward movement remains balanced.
Whether the shorter flight is recognised early.
Whether the player changes direction efficiently.
Whether acceleration is direct.
Whether the marker reaches the football’s line.
Whether the mark is completed in front.
Whether the lane remains safe.

commonErrors.error: The player leans backwards and cannot recover forward.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the hips underneath the body during the initial movement.

commonErrors.error: The marker takes several steps before changing direction.
commonErrors.correction: Use one controlled plant and turn immediately.

commonErrors.error: The player looks down during the turn.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the eyes on the football after release.

commonErrors.error: The marker approaches from beside the football’s line.
commonErrors.correction: Accelerate directly towards the receiving gate.

commonErrors.error: The player reaches while still off balance.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and establish a stable base.

commonErrors.error: The marker waits for the football to arrive.
commonErrors.correction: Attack forward and meet it before it drops.

progressions: Require a post-mark handball or kick.
regressions: Keep the receiving gate directly in front.
matchApplication: Players tracking deeper space may need to recover forward when a kick drops short. Early recognition and decisive forward movement can turn a difficult possession into a clean intercept or leading mark.
relatedDrills: MK-005 – Marking Footwork to the Football Line

title: Mark, Turn and Kick to a Lead
Marking Movement and Support Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing moving-mark execution, lead variety and support connection
objective: Assess each player’s ability to lead, change direction, track varied football flight, complete moving marks and connect with team support.
groundSize: Five assessment stations arranged within an area approximately sixty metres × forty metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert movement, support and technical assessment
setup:
Establish five assessment stations:
Station 1: Curved and stop-start lead marking.
Station 2: Backward-to-forward recovery marking.
Station 3: Moving mark followed by handball or kick.
Station 4: Lead replacement and lane-switch possession.
Station 5: Continuous end-to-end marking wave.
Divide players evenly between stations.
Assign a coach or trained observer where possible.
Standardise distances and delivery difficulty.
Allow one practice repetition before assessment.
Record movement, marking and post-mark execution separately.
Plan suitable recovery before Station 5.
howTheDrillWorks:
At Station 1, each player completes two curved leads and two stop-start leads in both directions.
At Station 2, each player completes four backward-to-forward recovery marks.
At Station 3, each player completes two mark-and-handball and two mark-and-kick actions.
At Station 4, players complete lead-replacement and lane-switch roles within a group possession chain.
At Station 5, players complete a timed continuous marking wave.
Observers assess lead timing, acceleration, body control, flight judgement, hand position and security.
Post-mark scanning, disposal and support movement are also scored.
Clearly unsuitable deliveries are repeated.
Each player receives one movement strength and one priority development action.
Players repeat the station linked to their lowest score where workload permits.
coachingPoints: Assess movement before the football is released.
Record whether each lead creates genuine separation or a clear lane.
Observe deceleration and change-of-direction safety.
Assess whether the player reaches the football’s line.
Apply full marking standards under movement.
Record whether possession is secured before the next action.
Evaluate post-mark scanning and disposal.
Include movement after disposal and positional replacement.
Assess whether technique remains stable under repeated effort.
Feedback must identify one specific observable behaviour.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players time varied leads correctly.
Whether changes of pace and direction create space.
Whether recovery footwork remains balanced.
Whether football flight is tracked continuously.
Whether moving marks are completed cleanly.
Whether the football is secured before disposal.
Whether handball and kicking connections are accurate.
Whether players replace vacated space.
Whether repeated-effort marking quality remains stable.
Whether feedback is applied during reassessment.

commonErrors.error: Leads begin before the ball carrier is ready.
commonErrors.correction: Establish visual connection and move from clean possession.

commonErrors.error: Players change direction from an upright position.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips and shorten the final step before turning.

commonErrors.error: The marker reaches without moving onto the football’s line.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the feet and position the body behind or beneath the ball.

commonErrors.error: Players stop before moving marks.
commonErrors.correction: Continue through the receiving gate.

commonErrors.error: The next disposal begins before the mark is secured.
commonErrors.correction: Complete two-hand control before scanning or releasing.

commonErrors.error: Support players fail to replace vacated space.
commonErrors.correction: Move as soon as the lead opens the position.

commonErrors.error: Lane-switch patterns become congested.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain assigned width until beginning the next lead.

commonErrors.error: Technique deteriorates during the continuous wave.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce workload and restore correct marking preparation.

progressions: Add live choice between multiple support options.
Repeat the assessment later and compare results.
regressions: Allow additional practice before formal scoring.
successIndicators: Connect accurately by hand or foot.
Maintain marking quality under repeated movement.
matchApplication: Moving marking depends on more than clean hands. Players must create space, track the football, secure possession, connect with support and continue contributing through repeated phases.

title: Off-Balance Mark Recovery
primarySkill: Securing or recovering possession after an off-balance marking attempt
objective: Develop the ability to remain involved when contact, flight or poor footing causes the player to lose balance during a marking attempt.
groundSize: Contest areas approximately twelve metres × ten metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced balance, recovery and safety management
setup:
Organise players into groups of three.
The feeder stands eight to ten metres away.
The marker begins inside the contest zone.
A pressure player starts beside the marker with a bump pad or controlled shoulder position.
The feeder delivers the football slightly away from the marker’s central line.
The pressure player applies controlled contact as the marker adjusts.
If the mark is not completed, the football remains live.
Rotate roles after four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers the football slightly left, right or overhead.
The marker adjusts towards the marking point.
The pressure player applies controlled legal contact.
The marker attempts to complete the mark.
If possession is secured, the player regains balance and exits.
If the football spills, the marker lands or regains the feet safely.
The player locates and attacks the loose football.
The pressure player competes under controlled rules.
The possession winner exits through a gate.
Players reset and rotate.
coachingPoints: Continue tracking the football when balance is disturbed.
Use short adjustment steps before contact.
Avoid reaching beyond a position that can be controlled.
Secure the football with two hands when possible.
Protect the head and body during landing.
Regain the feet before diving back into congestion.
Locate the football immediately.
Treat the second effort as part of the original contest.
Maintain safe contact throughout.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the marker continues tracking under contact.
Whether the player attempts an unsafe reach.
Whether landing technique remains controlled.
Whether the football is secured when possible.
Whether the player recovers quickly after a spill.
Whether the ground-ball contest remains safe.
Whether pressure intensity is appropriate.

commonErrors.error: The player reaches too far and falls uncontrollably.
commonErrors.correction: Move the feet further and remain within a balanced marking range.

commonErrors.error: The marker looks at the pressure player.
commonErrors.correction: Continue tracking the football through contact.

commonErrors.error: The player lands with locked legs.
commonErrors.correction: Flex the knees and absorb the landing.

commonErrors.error: The marker remains on the ground after a spill.
commonErrors.correction: Regain balance and locate the football immediately.

commonErrors.error: Players dive dangerously into the loose football.
commonErrors.correction: Approach under control and protect the head and shoulders.

commonErrors.error: Contact increases after the aerial phase.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish controlled ground-ball pressure rules.

progressions: Use a live opponent rather than a bump pad.
regressions: Practise landing and recovery without a football.
successIndicators: Track the football while off balance.
Land or regain balance under control.
matchApplication: Not every marking attempt occurs from a perfect position. Players must remain competitive after losing balance and be ready to win the resulting loose football.

title: High-Ball Turn-and-Compete
primarySkill: Turning, locating and contesting a high football against an opponent
objective: Develop the ability to begin facing away from the football, turn efficiently and compete for a high mark against an opponent reaching the contest from a different angle.
groundSize: Contest areas approximately twenty metres long and fourteen metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert turning, tracking and aerial-contest management
setup:
Position the feeder at one end of the area.
Two contest players begin facing away from the feeder.
Players start three to four metres apart.
Mark a drop zone eight to twelve metres behind them.
The coach gives a turn signal as the feeder delivers a high football.
Both players turn, locate and compete for the mark.
Contact is controlled and all spoil actions must target the football.
A fourth player assists with return and rotation.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both contest players begin facing the coach.
The coach gives the turn signal.
The feeder delivers a high football into the contest area.
Players turn over the most efficient shoulder and locate the ball.
Both accelerate towards the drop point.
Players establish legal position while tracking the football.
The advantaged player attempts to mark.
The other player attempts a legal spoil.
If the football spills, both compete at ground level.
Players reset and rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Turn through the hips and feet.
Locate the football before engaging the opponent.
Accelerate to the drop point.
Adjust speed as the flight becomes clear.
Use legal body position.
Mark when in front or spoil when behind.
Keep the eyes on the football.
Land and recover safely.
Continue until possession is won.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players turn efficiently.
Whether the football is located quickly.
Whether players reach the drop zone.
Whether bodywork remains legal.
Whether mark-or-spoil decisions are appropriate.
Whether landing remains safe.
Whether players compete after a spill.

commonErrors.error: Players engage each other before locating the football.
commonErrors.correction: Turn, find the flight and then establish position.

commonErrors.error: The player turns through the same shoulder every time.
commonErrors.correction: Use the direction that provides the fastest football location.

commonErrors.error: Both players sprint past the drop point.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust speed with shorter final steps.

commonErrors.error: The trailing player pushes rather than spoils.
commonErrors.correction: Attack the football with an open or clenched fist.

commonErrors.error: The advantaged player waits beneath the football.
commonErrors.correction: Take it at the highest comfortable point.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after landing.
commonErrors.correction: Locate the football immediately if the mark is incomplete.

progressions: Add a third player approaching from the side.
matchApplication: Players frequently turn from a forward-facing defensive or attacking position to compete for a kick travelling behind them. Quick football location is essential before body position can be established.

title: Complete Congestion and Contested Marking Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing marking performance under body pressure, congestion, repeated effort and live aerial competition
objective: Assess each player’s ability to track, position, mark, spoil, recover and transition across demanding contested-marking situations.
groundSize: Six assessment stations arranged across half a ground.
contact: 3 – Match-Like Contact, adjusted to age and competition level
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert assessment, contact and workload management
setup:
Establish six assessment stations:
Station 1: Drop-zone body protection.
Station 2: Leading mark with late contact.
Station 3: One-on-one mark-or-spoil contest.
Station 4: Two-versus-two and three-player pack contests.
Station 5: Repeat aerial contests.
Station 6: Intercept mark and defensive exit.
Divide players evenly between stations.
Match players appropriately for physical size and capacity.
Assign trained coaches or observers.
Explain legal contact, spoil, jump and landing standards.
Allow one practice repetition before formal scoring.
Schedule recovery before repeated and pack-contest stations.
Stop any unsafe repetition immediately.
howTheDrillWorks:
At Station 1, each player completes four drop-zone positioning contests.
At Station 2, each player completes four leading marks with controlled late pressure.
At Station 3, players complete four live one-on-one contests from varied starting positions.
At Station 4, players rotate through aerial, support and defensive pack roles.
At Station 5, players complete one block of four to six repeat aerial contests.
At Station 6, defenders complete four intercept decisions followed by rebound exits.
Observers score flight judgement, position, hand presentation, mark-or-spoil choice and security.
Landing safety, second effort and post-contest transition are also recorded.
Each player receives one contested-marking strength and one priority action.
Players repeat the lowest-scoring safe station where workload permits.
coachingPoints: Apply consistent legal contact standards.
Assess football tracking before and during body pressure.
Record whether the player identifies the drop zone.
Evaluate legal positioning and balance.
Assess mark-or-spoil decisions according to contest position.
Include aerial-role communication in multi-player contests.
Record landing safety and immediate second effort.
Judge whether possession is secured before disposal.
Assess intercept decisions as well as execution.
Feedback should identify a specific and observable improvement.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players identify football flight and drop point.
Whether legal position is established.
Whether players maintain strong hands under contact.
Whether mark-or-spoil decisions are appropriate.
Whether pack roles are communicated.
Whether players recover after spills.
Whether repeated-effort quality is maintained.
Whether intercept decisions are disciplined.
Whether post-contest exits are completed.
Whether coaching feedback is applied.

commonErrors.error: Players engage opponents before reading the football.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the flight and drop point first.

commonErrors.error: Position is maintained through holding or pushing.
commonErrors.correction: Use active feet and legal torso positioning.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt marks from clearly inferior positions.
commonErrors.correction: Spoil when clean possession is unrealistic.

commonErrors.error: Teammates compete against each other in packs.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate one aerial player and one ground-level player.

commonErrors.error: Landing technique deteriorates under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce workload and restore controlled knee flexion.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after incomplete marks.
commonErrors.correction: Continue immediately into the second contest.

commonErrors.error: The intercept defender leaves for an unreachable football.
commonErrors.correction: Assess distance and opponent position before committing.

commonErrors.error: Possession is lost during the exit.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the mark or recovery before beginning disposal.

progressions: Use opposition-specific forward and defensive roles.
Repeat the assessment later in the season.
matchApplication: Contested marking requires technical skill, body positioning, decision making, courage and repeated effort. This assessment determines whether players can compete safely and effectively when the football, opponents and support roles are all live.

title: Centre Clearance Marking Chain
primarySkill: Connecting a centre-clearance possession through consecutive forward marks
objective: Develop a structured marking chain that converts centre-clearance possession into a controlled forward entry before the opposition establishes its defensive shape.
groundSize: An area extending from the centre square to inside forward 50.
setup:
Establish a centre-square starting position.
Position Player A as the clearance winner or first receiver.
Position Player B as the first midfield marking option.
Position Player C as a high-half-forward connection.
Position Players D and E as separate inside 50 targets.
Mark receiving gates through the midfield, half-forward and forward lines.
Add shadow defenders who may close one lead in each line.
Rotate players through clearance, midfield, half-forward and forward roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A begins with possession from a controlled centre-clearance feed.
Player B leads into the first midfield gate.
Player A kicks into Player B’s forward movement.
Player C begins the high-half-forward lead after Player B marks.
Player B secures possession, scans and connects with Player C.
Players D and E create separate inside 50 leads.
Player C reads the defensive positioning and selects the advantaged forward.
The football is kicked into the selected lead.
The forward completes the mark or contests the delivery.
Players reset through external recovery lanes.
coachingPoints: The first marking option should move possession forward rather than sideways.
Leads must begin from the previous clean possession.
Midfield and half-forward players should operate at different depths.
Inside 50 leads must remain separated.
Ball carriers should scan before receiving where possible.
Deliver every kick to the receiver’s advantage.
Avoid adding an unnecessary marking possession once a direct forward entry is available.
Unused players must remain connected as support.
React immediately if the possession is intercepted.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the first lead begins immediately.
Whether midfield and half-forward depths remain separated.
Whether players secure the mark before turning.
Whether forward leads are coordinated.
Whether the correct target is selected.
Whether the football reaches the receiver’s advantage.
Whether unused players continue supporting.
Whether turnover transition is immediate.

commonErrors.error: The first receiver leads sideways and slows the clearance.
commonErrors.correction: Attack a forward-facing midfield gate.

commonErrors.error: The half-forward leads before the midfield mark is completed.
commonErrors.correction: Begin movement from clean possession.

commonErrors.error: Both forwards lead into the same space.
commonErrors.correction: Assign separate front, lateral and deeper lanes.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier kicks to the preferred teammate rather than the advantaged option.
commonErrors.correction: Scan defensive positioning before selecting the target.

commonErrors.error: The football is delivered behind the lead.
commonErrors.correction: Release earlier and target the forward edge of the gate.

commonErrors.error: Unused players stop after the kick.
commonErrors.correction: Reposition beneath or outside the next possession.

progressions: Add active midfield and forward defenders.
Begin from a live centre bounce.
regressions: Begin from a stationary midfield possession.
matchApplication: Centre-clearance possession is most dangerous when the football moves forward before defensive structure forms. Consecutive marks through midfield and half-forward can create a high-quality scoring opportunity.

title: Disguised Lead and Late Break Mark
Elite Marking Decision and Execution Assessment
Kick-In Marking Exit Scenario
primarySkill: Creating and completing marking options from a defensive kick-in
objective: Develop a coordinated kick-in marking structure that provides short, wide, long and reset options while protecting the most dangerous turnover areas.
groundSize: Defensive 50 extending to approximately twenty metres beyond the arc.
equipment: Short, wide, long and reset gates
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert kick-in structure and defensive-risk management
setup:
Position the kicker inside the goal square.
Place receivers in four roles:
Short pocket option.
Wide half-back option.
Long boundary option.
Central or behind-ball reset option.
Organise the opposition in a selected kick-in press.
Mark a dangerous central turnover zone directly in front of goal.
Allow the kicker to play on where appropriate.
Position secondary marking targets beyond defensive 50.
Rotate kickers, receivers and pressing roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach signals a behind and places the football with the kicker.
Defensive players spread into assigned marking lanes.
The opposition establishes the selected press.
The kicker scans short, wide, long and reset options.
Receivers adjust their leads according to the press.
The kicker selects and delivers to the safest useful marker.
The receiver completes and secures the mark.
The next defensive line creates a second marking connection.
A turnover remains live and allows the opposition to attack goal.
Players reset and repeat from varied pressing structures.
coachingPoints: Spread immediately after the behind is scored.
Receivers should operate at different widths and depths.
The short option must not draw the football into the centre of goal.
Wide players should maintain separation from the boundary trap.
Long targets require ground-level support.
The kicker should not play on automatically.
Use a firm and accurate kick.
Secure the first mark before continuing.
The second marking option should prepare before the first kick is taken.
Avoid dangerous central turnovers.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defensive spread occurs quickly.
Whether options appear at different depths.
Whether the kicker scans the complete structure.
Whether the press affects the decision.
Whether dangerous central kicks are rejected.
Whether the first mark is completed.
Whether the next marking connection appears early.
Whether turnover reaction is immediate.

commonErrors.error: Receivers move before the kicker is ready and become stationary.
commonErrors.correction: Time leads from the kicker’s control and scanning position.

commonErrors.error: All options appear on the same side.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain width on both sides and support behind the football.

commonErrors.error: The kicker plays on directly into pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Assess the first defensive line before leaving the square.

commonErrors.error: The first kick enters the central danger zone.
commonErrors.correction: Use a safer wide or boundary-side marking lane.

commonErrors.error: Long targets fly without ground-level support.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate one aerial player and position teammates for the spill.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after the first mark.
commonErrors.correction: Prepare the second connection before the kick-in is delivered.

progressions: Change the opposition press between repetitions.
Add a kick-in play-on time limit.
Require a full exit beyond the centre.
regressions: Finish after the first exit mark.
matchApplication: Kick-ins require coordinated marking movement before the opposition press settles. The first mark should protect field position while creating the next exit opportunity.

title: Centre-Bounce Forward Marking Surge
primarySkill: Creating and completing a forward mark immediately after centre-bounce possession
objective: Develop a rapid marking connection from centre-bounce possession into forward 50 before the opposition’s defensive structure is established.
groundSize: Centre square through to the full forward 50.
setup:
Organise a controlled centre-bounce or coach-fed clearance.
Position midfielders in realistic stoppage roles.
Position one high-half-forward connection option.
Position three forwards in separate central, lateral and deep lanes.
Assign direct defenders and one spare defender.
Mark high-half-forward and inside 50 receiving gates.
Keep one attacking player at ground level beneath the final contest.
Rotate all positional roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach starts the centre-bounce or clearance phase.
One midfielder wins or receives the first clean possession.
The high-half-forward presents if a direct forward kick is unavailable.
Forwards hold separate lanes until the ball carrier is balanced.
The ball carrier selects the clearest marking option.
The football is delivered into the lead.
The selected forward completes or strongly contests the mark.
Ground-level forwards position for a spill.
A completed mark leads to a shot; a defensive win launches transition.
Players reset and repeat with different clearance directions.
coachingPoints: Forward movement should begin from a clean clearance rather than the initial ruck contest.
Avoid every forward leading towards the same point.
The high-half-forward should connect only when required.
Direct forward access should be used when clearly available.
Deliver before defenders recover into the lane.
Kick to the protected side of the receiver.
Maintain one ground-level player.
The unused forward should continue supporting.
React immediately to a defensive intercept or spoil.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether forward leads are timed from clean possession.
Whether forwards maintain separation.
Whether the high-half-forward connects appropriately.
Whether the ball carrier scans before disposal.
Whether delivery favours the marker.
Whether ground-level support is organised.
Whether the possession creates a genuine scoring opportunity.
Whether defensive transition begins immediately.

commonErrors.error: Forwards begin leading before the clearance is controlled.
commonErrors.correction: Hold structure until the ball carrier has clean possession.

commonErrors.error: Every forward leads directly at the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain central, lateral and deep lanes.

commonErrors.error: The high-half-forward crowds the inside 50 space.
commonErrors.correction: Present only when a connection mark is required.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier holds too long and allows defenders to recover.
commonErrors.correction: Deliver once a clear advantage appears.

commonErrors.error: The kick favours the defender.
commonErrors.correction: Place the football to the receiver’s protected side.

commonErrors.error: All forwards fly for the final football.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate the primary aerial player and retain ground-level support.

progressions: Add scoreboard requirements after conceding a goal.
Allow handball or carry before the entry.
Continue until the possession produces a score or turnover exit.
regressions: Begin from a stationary midfield possession.
Finish after the forward marking attempt.
successIndicators: Win or receive clean clearance possession.
Complete or strongly contest the mark.
matchApplication: Centre-bounce wins create a brief opportunity to attack an unsettled defence. Coordinated forward marking movement can turn the clearance into an immediate score.

title: Defensive Intercept Chain Under Repeat Entry
Forward-Half Marking Lock-In
primarySkill: Using forward-half marking and interception to retain attacking territory
objective: Develop the ability to prevent an opposition exit, complete intercept marks in the forward half and convert retained possession into a new scoring opportunity.
equipment: Defensive exit and attacking entry gates
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert forward-half structure and transition management
setup:
Position the attacking team across forward 50 and the high-forward area.
Position the defending team with the football after a mark or behind.
Mark three defensive exit lanes.
Position attacking intercept players between those lanes.
Position forwards in separated scoring lead zones.
The defending team attempts to exit through a mark.
The attacking team attempts to intercept or spoil the exit.
On retained possession, forwards reorganise immediately.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defending team begins from a mark inside defensive 50.
Defensive receivers create exit marking options.
Attacking players position to pressure and intercept.
The football is kicked towards an exit option.
The attacking team attempts to complete an intercept mark or controlled spoil.
On retained possession, the mark winner secures and scans.
Forwards create separate scoring leads.
The football is re-entered to the advantaged target.
A successful defensive exit ends the repetition.
Teams reset and rotate positional roles.
coachingPoints: Forward-half interceptors should protect the most likely exit lanes.
Avoid every attacker chasing the ball carrier.
One player pressures while others hold interception positions.
Mark the football cleanly when possible.
Spoil towards attacking support when a mark is unrealistic.
Secure an intercept before rushing the re-entry.
Forwards must spread immediately after possession is retained.
Avoid kicking back into the same crowded contest.
Use a high-forward reset if no scoring lead is open.
Defenders should maintain short, wide and long exit options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether attacking pressure and interception roles are separated.
Whether likely exit lanes are covered.
Whether intercept marks are completed.
Whether spoils are directed to attacking support.
Whether forwards reorganise after retained possession.
Whether the re-entry creates advantage.
Whether defenders provide multiple exit options.
Whether the repetition ends with a score or successful exit.

commonErrors.error: Every attacking player pressures the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Assign one pressure player and maintain interception coverage.

commonErrors.error: Interceptors stand directly behind defensive receivers.
commonErrors.correction: Position inside or ahead of the expected kicking lane.

commonErrors.error: The intercept winner kicks immediately into congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession, scan and use a reset if required.

commonErrors.error: Forwards remain in the original marking contest.
commonErrors.correction: Spread into new scoring lanes after possession is retained.

commonErrors.error: Spoils are directed towards defensive support.
commonErrors.correction: Aim towards attacking teammates or safe boundary space.

commonErrors.error: Defenders use only one exit side.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain short, wide and opposite-side marking options.

progressions: Begin from kick-ins and defensive intercepts.
Limit the defending team’s disposal time.
successIndicators: Complete intercept marks or effective spoils.
matchApplication: Strong teams retain attacking territory by combining pressure with intercept positioning. A forward-half mark can create a higher-quality second entry than the original possession.
relatedDrills: MK-059 – Intercept Mark Under Forward Pressure
MK-079 – Continuous Team Marking Possession Game

title: Strong-Wind Marking Adjustment Scenario
primarySkill: Adjusting marking movement and technique to strong or changing wind
objective: Develop the ability to read wind-affected football flight, reposition to the true drop point and select appropriate marking and disposal options.
groundSize: A possession area approximately forty metres × thirty metres aligned across and with the prevailing wind.
setup:
Mark stations for:
Kicking with the wind.
Kicking into the wind.
Kicking across the wind.
Use natural wind where available.
When conditions are calm, feeders deliberately shape controlled drifting footballs.
Position markers and defenders in each lane.
Add ground-level support players.
Mark adjusted receiving zones rather than fixed central targets.
Rotate all players through each wind relationship.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder identifies the wind relationship.
The marker begins from a neutral starting position.
The football is kicked with, against or across the wind.
The marker reads the early flight.
The player adjusts towards the likely true drop point.
The defender applies controlled pressure.
The marker selects chest, overhead, low or ground-level recovery technique.
Possession is secured and moved through an exit gate.
If the football spills, support players compete for the next possession.
Players rotate to a different wind station.
coachingPoints: Observe wind direction before the football is kicked.
Expect the football to carry further with the wind.
Expect it to drop shorter into the wind.
Move across the flight line when the wind shifts the football laterally.
Avoid standing directly beneath the initial projected drop point.
Use active adjustment steps until contact.
Maintain two-hand marking technique.
Ground-level players should anticipate front or side spills.
Kicking options should use trajectories suited to the wind.
Safety remains the priority in severe conditions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players identify wind direction.
Whether they adjust early enough.
Whether players run under or past the football.
Whether hand position matches the final height.
Whether defenders also read the flight.
Whether ground-level support positions effectively.
Whether kick trajectories suit the conditions.
Whether players communicate environmental information.

commonErrors.error: The marker runs to the initial flight line and stops.
commonErrors.correction: Continue adjusting until the true drop point is clear.

commonErrors.error: Players underestimate football carry with the wind.
commonErrors.correction: Begin deeper and reduce forward momentum earlier.

commonErrors.error: Players wait too deep when kicking into the wind.
commonErrors.correction: Attack forward as the football drops shorter.

commonErrors.error: Cross-wind movement is recognised too late.
commonErrors.correction: Move laterally during the early flight.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt one-handed marks in unstable flight.
commonErrors.correction: Present two hands and secure the football firmly.

commonErrors.error: Ground-level teammates assume the mark will be completed.
commonErrors.correction: Position for likely wind-affected spills.

progressions: Add scoreboard scenarios favouring one end.
Require players to choose the correct side of the ground.
Introduce wet and windy conditions together where safe.
regressions: Practise one wind relationship at a time.
matchApplication: Wind changes football depth, lateral movement and drop speed. Players who read conditions earlier can establish position while opponents react to the initial flight.

title: Tag-Release Marking Scenario
primarySkill: Using marking movement to release a closely tagged player
objective: Develop coordinated marking movement that helps a closely checked midfielder or forward create separation without illegal blocking.
groundSize: Stations approximately thirty metres long and twenty-five metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert off-ball movement and legal-spacing management
setup:
Position Player A as the ball carrier.
Position Player B as the tagged player.
Position Defender 1 in close checking position on Player B.
Position Players C and D as supporting markers.
Position Defenders 2 and 3 on the support players.
Mark separate short, crossing and late-release gates.
Supporting players use movement to create traffic and change defensive relationships without blocking.
Player B times the release into the space created.
Rotate all roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A gains possession.
Players C and D begin coordinated leads through separate lanes.
Their movement shifts defenders and creates new space.
Player B delays while reading Defender 1.
When a legal release lane opens, Player B accelerates.
Player A identifies the movement and delivers into the lead.
Player B completes and secures the mark.
Supporting players replace behind or outside possession.
If the tagger maintains coverage, Player A uses another open marker.
Players reset and rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Supporting movement must remain legal.
Players may occupy space but must not hold, push or deliberately impede defenders.
The tagged player should delay until teammates affect the defensive shape.
Accelerate sharply once the lane opens.
The ball carrier should not focus exclusively on the tagged player.
Use another free marker if the release does not occur.
Deliver to the protected side.
Support should replace behind the completed mark.
Continue varying release methods.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether supporting leads remain legal.
Whether defenders are moved.
Whether the tagged player delays appropriately.
Whether the release lane is recognised.
Whether the ball carrier scans all options.
Whether the kick protects the receiver.
Whether the tagger maintains legal pressure.
Whether support continues after the mark.

commonErrors.error: Supporting players deliberately block the tagger.
commonErrors.correction: Use legitimate leads and occupy space without initiating illegal contact.

commonErrors.error: The tagged player leads before teammate movement develops.
commonErrors.correction: Delay until the defensive relationship changes.

commonErrors.error: The player jogs from the tag.
commonErrors.correction: Accelerate sharply once the release lane opens.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier forces the tagged option.
commonErrors.correction: Use another open marker when the tagger maintains coverage.

commonErrors.error: Supporting players crowd the final receiving lane.
commonErrors.correction: Clear or replace after creating the release.

commonErrors.error: The kick is delivered to the tagger’s side.
commonErrors.correction: Place the football to the receiver’s protected shoulder.

matchApplication: Closely checked players often require coordinated teammate movement to create space. The release must come from legal leading patterns rather than illegal blocking.
relatedDrills: MK-081 – Disguised Lead and Late Break Mark

title: Mark-to-Handball Transition Decision Game
primarySkill: Selecting whether to retain marking possession or transition immediately into handball movement
objective: Develop the ability to complete a mark and choose whether the next phase should remain a marking possession or shift into a handball-based transition.
groundSize: A directional area approximately thirty-five metres × twenty-five metres.
setup:
Position one ball carrier and two marking receivers.
Position one run-past support player.
Position two defenders who may close marking or handball lanes.
Mark:
One retention-mark gate.
One forward-mark gate.
One handball-release gate.
The first receiver completes a mark.
The defender’s position determines whether the next action remains a kick or becomes a handball release.
Rotate all roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
Player A kicks to Player B’s lead.
Player B completes and secures the mark.
Player C begins a run-past support movement.
Defenders adjust to close either the kick or handball lane.
Player B scans immediate pressure and support.
If Player C is free, Player B handballs into the running path.
If the handball lane is closed, Player B uses a marking option ahead or outside.
If both forward options close, Player B retains or resets possession.
Play continues through the selected exit gate.
Players reset and rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Complete the mark before changing disposal mode.
Scan pressure immediately.
The support runner should time movement from the clean mark.
A handball should create speed or numerical advantage.
Do not handball merely because a teammate runs past.
Maintain marking possession when the kick remains the better option.
Retain or reset when both forward lanes are closed.
Protect the football from the pressure side.
Execute every disposal from balance.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the mark is secured.
Whether the run-past support is timed.
Whether defenders affect the decision.
Whether the player selects kick, handball or retention appropriately.
Whether the handball leads the runner.
Whether marking options remain available.
Whether the football is protected.
Whether the next possession maintains advantage.

commonErrors.error: The player prepares the handball before completing the mark.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession with two hands first.

commonErrors.error: The support runner arrives before the mark.
commonErrors.correction: Begin the run from clean possession.

commonErrors.error: The marker handballs automatically.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm that the release creates genuine advantage.

commonErrors.error: The player ignores an open marking option.
commonErrors.correction: Scan kick and handball lanes before deciding.

commonErrors.error: The marker plays on when both lanes are closed.
commonErrors.correction: Hold or use behind-ball support.

commonErrors.error: The handball is released behind the runner.
commonErrors.correction: Strike earlier into the forward path.

progressions: Continue into a full scoring phase.
successIndicators: Select kick, handball or retention appropriately.
matchApplication: A mark may slow play or create a platform for immediate handball transition. The correct choice depends on pressure, support and the advantage created by the next possession.
relatedDrills: MK-034 – Moving Mark and Immediate Handball
MK-086 – Mark, Hold or Play-On Decision

title: Player-Led Marking Scenario Challenge
primarySkill: Designing and solving marking scenarios through player-led tactical decisions
objective: Develop player ownership by requiring teams to organise, execute and review solutions to complex marking scenarios without continuous coach direction.
groundSize: Half to full ground depending on the selected scenarios.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert facilitation and player-led review management
setup:
Prepare scenario cards such as:
Escape a kick-in press.
Protect a narrow lead.
Create a forward mark against a spare defender.
Break a corridor zone.
Defend repeat entries.
Retain possession while one player down.
Divide players into two teams.
Select leadership groups for each scenario.
Give teams a limited planning period.
Coaches provide rules and safety boundaries but do not prescribe the solution.
Use realistic match positioning and contact.
howTheDrillWorks:
A scenario card is presented to both teams.
Each leadership group receives a short planning period.
Players organise marking, defensive and support roles.
The scenario begins from the nominated restart.
Teams execute their chosen solutions.
Play remains live until the scenario outcome is reached.
Players review what occurred without immediate coach correction.
The leadership group identifies one change.
The scenario is repeated.
Coaches conclude with targeted feedback linked to player observations.
coachingPoints: Players must identify the scenario’s primary problem.
Solutions should define width, depth, aerial roles and risk.
Leadership communication must be clear and concise.
Every player should understand the intended marking structure.
Adaptation during play is encouraged.
Marking technique and legal contact standards remain unchanged.
Reviews should focus on decisions and movement rather than blame.
One practical change should be selected before the repeat.
Coaches should guide with questions rather than supply every answer.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether leaders identify the key problem.
Whether plans include marking support and aerial roles.
Whether all players understand the plan.
Whether communication continues during play.
Whether players adapt when the opposition changes.
Whether technical execution supports the plan.
Whether reviews are accurate and constructive.
Whether the selected adjustment improves the repeated scenario.

commonErrors.error: The team creates an overly complex plan.
commonErrors.correction: Select two or three clear marking principles.

commonErrors.error: Only the leadership group understands the structure.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm every positional line knows its role.

commonErrors.error: Players continue the original plan after conditions change.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and adapt to the live defensive response.

commonErrors.error: Reviews focus only on skill errors.
commonErrors.correction: Discuss spacing, timing, risk and role execution as well.

commonErrors.error: Players blame individuals for the outcome.
commonErrors.correction: Focus on repeatable team behaviours.

commonErrors.error: The second attempt repeats the same problem.
commonErrors.correction: Identify one specific change before restarting.

progressions: Allow players to design their own scenario.
regressions: Allow one coach question during planning.
matchApplication: Players must solve marking and possession problems during matches without waiting for coaches. Player-led scenario work builds communication, ownership and tactical adaptability.

title: Complete Marking Chapter Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing complete marking development from fundamental technique to elite match application
objective: Complete a comprehensive chapter assessment that measures individual marking technique, movement, contested performance, positional application, team structure and match-scenario decision making.
groundSize: Full ground or multiple connected assessment areas covering technical, contested and team phases.
equipment: Lead, contest, reset, exit and scoring gates
contact: 3 – Match-Like Contact, adjusted to age, experience and competition level
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert whole-chapter assessment and safety management
setup:
Establish six complete assessment phases:
Phase 1: Fundamental chest, overhead and low marking.
Phase 2: Moving, leading and change-of-direction marking.
Phase 3: Pressure, bodywork and contested marking.
Phase 4: Intercept, positional and aerial-role marking.
Phase 5: Team marking movement and possession systems.
Phase 6: Full-ground match-scenario simulation.
Divide players into suitable groups.
Assign trained observers to each phase.
Match players appropriately for contact and aerial contests.
Standardise technical deliveries where formal comparison is required.
Explain scoring criteria before beginning.
Record technical execution, decision quality and team impact separately.
Plan recovery before contested and full-ground phases.
howTheDrillWorks:
In Phase 1, players complete chest, overhead, low and one-grab marking assessments.
In Phase 2, players complete straight, angled, lateral, double and backward-flight marking tasks.
In Phase 3, players rotate through front-position, side-by-side, high-ball and ground-recovery contests.
In Phase 4, players complete intercept, fly-or-stay, spare-defender and position-specific marking scenarios.
In Phase 5, teams execute defensive exits, switches, midfield connections and forward marking patterns.
In Phase 6, teams complete a live scoreboard or game-plan simulation.
Coaches score tracking, footwork, hand position, security, contact management, movement and tactical selection.
Players receive one technical strength, one tactical strength and two priority actions.
Groups repeat one selected task linked to their most important development need.
Finish with a player and coach review of the complete marking chapter.
coachingPoints: Apply age-appropriate standards in every phase.
Fundamental marking quality remains relevant in advanced scenarios.
Assess whether feet position the body before the hands attempt the mark.
Judge hand position according to football height.
Record one-grab control and post-contact security.
Evaluate lead timing and separation.
Assess bodywork for legality and balance.
Include mark-or-spoil and fly-or-stay decisions.
Record landing safety and second effort.
Evaluate intercept decisions as well as completed marks.
Assess team width, depth and support before possession.
Judge marking decisions according to score, time and field position.
Separate poor delivery from player error.
Feedback must be observable and actionable.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players apply correct fundamental technique.
Whether moving players reach the football’s line.
Whether leads create genuine separation.
Whether contact remains legal and balanced.
Whether aerial roles are communicated.
Whether players recover after incomplete marks.
Whether intercept decisions are disciplined.
Whether position-specific roles are understood.
Whether team marking shape provides width and depth.
Whether post-mark decisions create advantage.
Whether scoreboard and scenario context affects risk.
Whether feedback is applied during reassessment.

commonErrors.error: Players rely on the body rather than meeting the football with the hands.
commonErrors.correction: Present two hands and contact the football before it reaches the torso.

commonErrors.error: Hand position does not match the football’s height.
commonErrors.correction: Use fingers down for low marks and thumbs behind for chest and overhead marks.

commonErrors.error: Players reach without adjusting the feet.
commonErrors.correction: Move behind or beneath the football before attempting the mark.

commonErrors.error: Moving markers stop before contact.
commonErrors.correction: Continue through the receiving line and secure possession in motion.

commonErrors.error: Players use illegal holds or pushes in contested marks.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain position through active feet and legal bodywork.

commonErrors.error: Multiple teammates fly for the same football.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate one aerial player and one or more ground-level roles.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after a spoiled or dropped mark.
commonErrors.correction: Recover immediately into the second contest.

commonErrors.error: Intercept players leave for unreachable footballs.
commonErrors.correction: Assess flight, distance and opponent position before committing.

commonErrors.error: Team marking options operate at the same depth.
commonErrors.correction: Create short, wide, behind and forward support layers.

commonErrors.error: Mark winners automatically play on.
commonErrors.correction: Scan pressure, support, score, time and field position first.

commonErrors.error: Teams force central marks despite interception risk.
commonErrors.correction: Use width, reset or behind-ball support when the corridor is closed.

commonErrors.error: Technical quality collapses under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce workload and restore correct tracking, footwork and two-hand control.

progressions: Use full match-like contact for prepared players.
Introduce changing scoreboard and numerical scenarios.
Complete video-supported individual and positional reviews.
Repeat the assessment later in the season to measure development.
regressions: Assess each phase on separate training nights.
Provide additional practice before formal scoring.
Remove advanced aerial work for unsuitable players.
successIndicators: Execute secure chest, overhead and low marks.
Use effective footwork and hand position.
Select mark, spoil and fly-or-stay appropriately.
Land safely and recover after spills.
Create team marking support at varied widths and depths.
Maintain technical quality under pressure and fatigue.
matchApplication: Complete marking performance combines technical hands, movement, body positioning, aerial judgement, positional responsibility, team structure and match awareness. This assessment confirms whether players can transfer the full marking chapter into competitive football.
relatedDrills: MK-050 – Pressure and Contested Marking Assessment
MK-100 – Elite Marking Decision and Execution Assessment
